hints: Recall the two families of substituents in electrophilic substitution, those that push electrons into the ring and those that pull electrons away.
walkthrough:
Sort directors into two types**
Think of substituents already on benzene as traffic signs. Groups like $-OH$, $-NH_2$ and alkyl push electrons toward the ring and direct ortho and para. Groups that pull electrons away do the opposite.

Place the nitro group**
The $-NO_2$ group has very electronegative N and O atoms pulling electron density out of the ring. That deactivates ortho and para attack more than meta, so incoming electrophiles go to the meta, 3 and 5, positions.
Final answer: The $-NO_2$ group is a meta director to positions 3 and 5, because it is a strongly electron withdrawing group.

hints: Think of concentrated $H_2SO_4$ acting as an acid toward $HNO_3$ acting as a base to generate a cation plus an anion plus water.
walkthrough:
See the role of the acids**
You need the powerful electrophile $NO_2^+$. Nitric acid alone is not enough. Sulfuric acid, the stronger acid, protonates nitric acid, which then loses water.

Balance the formation**
$HNO_3$ gains $H^+$ from $H_2SO_4$ to give $H_2NO_3^+$, which splits to $NO_2^+$ and $H_2O$. The $H_2SO_4$ becomes $HSO_4^-$. That gives: $$HNO_3 + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow NO_2^+ + HSO_4^- + H_2O$$

hints: Compare compound Q with benzene and notice it has two new C-C bonded groups meta to each other, an ethanoyl group and a 1-methylethyl group, so ask which group must be added first to direct meta.
walkthrough:
Read Q backwards**
Look at Q. At the top is $COCH_3$ and at the bottom right is $CH(CH_3)_2$, meta to each other. Both were added by electrophilic substitution, but the order matters.

Choose the director that gives meta**
The $COCH_3$ group is electron withdrawing and meta directing, while an alkyl group is ortho and para directing. To get the second group meta to the first, you must put the $COCH_3$ on first. So P is just benzene with $COCH_3$: $$C_6H_6 \rightarrow C_6H_5COCH_3$$
Final answer: Compound P is phenylethanone, $C_6H_5COCH_3$ (benzene ring bonded to $C(=O)CH_3$).

hints: Recall that forming a $C_6H_5COCH_3$ from benzene needs an acyl electrophile generated from an acyl chloride with an aluminium chloride catalyst.
Recall that adding a $CH(CH_3)_2$ group to the ring needs the corresponding haloalkane electrophile with a catalyst that can polarise a C-Br bond.
walkthrough:
Build P by acylation**
Reaction 1 is Friedel Crafts acylation. Ethanoyl chloride provides the $CH_3CO^+$ electrophile when polarised by the Lewis acid catalyst $AlCl_3$: $$C_6H_6 + CH_3COCl \xrightarrow{AlCl_3} C_6H_5COCH_3 + HCl$$

Build Q by alkylation**
Reaction 2 is Friedel Crafts alkylation on deactivated P. 2-bromopropane, $(CH_3)_2CHBr$, provides the isopropyl electrophile with $FeBr_3$ (or $AlBr_3$) as catalyst. Because $COCH_3$ is meta directing, the alkyl group enters meta to give Q.

Final answer: reaction 1: $CH_3COCl$ and $AlCl_3$
reaction 2: $(CH_3)_2CHBr$ and $FeBr_3$

hints: Recall what warm $AgNO_3(aq)$ tests for, free halide ions forming $AgBr$ precipitate, and ask which C-Br bond can hydrolyse to release $Br^-$.
Compare the position of Br, directly attached to the ring in $C_6H_5Br$ versus attached to a side chain $CH_2$ in $C_6H_5CH_2Br$.
Think about what the lone pair on Br directly attached to the ring can do with the benzene pi system and how that changes C-Br bond strength.
walkthrough:
Link observation to hydrolysis**
Warm $AgNO_3(aq)$ only gives a precipitate if $Br^-$ is released into solution by hydrolysis: $$RBr + H_2O \rightarrow ROH + Br^- + H^+$$ followed by $$Ag^+ + Br^- \rightarrow AgBr(s)$$ cream. So you are really testing how easily the C-Br bond breaks.

Contrast the two structures**
In $C_6H_5CH_2Br$ the Br is on a side chain, a benzylic bromide. The C-Br is a normal single bond and hydrolyses readily on warming, so cream $AgBr$ appears. In $C_6H_5Br$ the Br is directly on the ring, an aryl bromide.

Explain the aryl resistance**
Picture Br attached to benzene. One of its p orbitals holding a lone pair can overlap sideways with the delocalised pi system of the ring. That lone pair is drawn into the ring. This gives the C-Br bond partial double bond character, making it shorter and stronger, so hydrolysis does not occur and no precipitate forms.

Final answer: $C_6H_5Br$ with $AgNO_3(aq)$: no change, no precipitate.
$C_6H_5CH_2Br$ with $AgNO_3(aq)$: cream precipitate of $AgBr$.
Explanation: in $C_6H_5Br$ a lone pair on Br overlaps with the ring pi system, delocalised into the ring, giving the C-Br bond partial double bond character so it is stronger and does not hydrolyse.

hints: Recall the two stage name used for acyl chlorides with nucleophiles like water, first attack at $C=O$ then loss of halide.
walkthrough:
Name the two stages**
Water first adds to the $C=O$ carbon to give a tetrahedral intermediate, then the $Br^-$ leaving group is eliminated to reform $C=O$. That is nucleophilic addition followed by elimination.
Final answer: (nucleophilic) addition-elimination

hints: Start by identifying the nucleophile atom in $H_2O$ and the electrophilic carbon in $RCOBr$, remembering to show the $C^{\delta+}$ $O^{\delta-}$ dipole.
Think where the curly arrow from the $C=O$ pi bond must go when the new O-C bond forms.
Draw the charge on each oxygen in the tetrahedral intermediate formed after addition, one from the original carbonyl and one from the incoming water.
For the second stage, ask which lone pair reforms the $C=O$ and which bond must break to expel bromide.
walkthrough:
Set up the nucleophilic attack**
Find the reactive centres. O in $H_2O$ has two lone pairs and is the nucleophile. C in $R-C(=O)-Br$ is $C^{\delta+}$ because O pulls electrons away, shown as $C^{\delta+}=O^{\delta-}$. Draw a curly arrow from a lone pair on O to the $C^{\delta+}$.

Break the pi bond**
As the new O-C bond forms, carbon would have too many bonds. The $C=O$ pi pair moves onto O. Draw a curly arrow from the $C=O$ bond to the O atom, giving $O^-$. This is addition.

Draw the tetrahedral intermediate**
You now have carbon bonded to four groups: $R$, $Br$, $O^-$ (original carbonyl O) and $OH_2^+$ (the incoming water O now with two H and a positive formal charge). That is: $$R-C(Br)(O^-)(OH_2^+)$$ Show all lone pairs, charges and the tetrahedral shape.

Eliminate bromide to reform the carbonyl**
Now reform $C=O$. Draw a curly arrow from the lone pair on $O^-$ back to form a $C=O$ double bond, and a curly arrow from the $C-Br$ bond onto Br to expel $Br^-$. After proton transfer this gives carboxylic acid $RCOOH$ plus $HBr$. This is elimination.

Final answer: Step 1: lone pair on O of $H_2O$ attacks $C^{\delta+}$ of $C^{\delta+}=O^{\delta-}$; curly arrow $C=O$ to O to give $O^-$.
Intermediate: $R-C(Br)(O^-)(OH_2^+)$, tetrahedral with $O^-$ and $^+OH_2$ groups.
Step 2: lone pair on $O^-$ reforms $C=O$, curly arrow $C-Br$ to $Br^-$ to give $RCOOH + HBr$.
